prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock rests on one simple physical trick: at the magic wavelength the trapping light shifts both clock levels equally, so thousands of neutral atoms can be held and interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil broadening. This took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18 and gave a new instrument that sees gravitational redshift over millimetres, tests the constancy of constants and underpins the coming redefinition of the second. The consequences follow from the science and not from a technological brief, which is the kind of discovery I value. Seven of eight members ranked it, five put it in their top three, and the support comes from members with quite different fields (Kroll, Olsson, Danielsson, Pearce, Eriksson), which tells me it is not only an atomic-physics preference. Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, China) operate lattice clocks and agree at the 1e-18 level, so reproducibility, which I weigh heavily, is excellent. The attribution is also the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first strontium realisation, Ye for taking it to the accuracy and stability frontier and for the many-body clock physics.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty relative to earlier prizes: the 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered single-ion control and ion clocks, and Ye's work builds on the comb. A committee could read the lattice clock as an extension of metrology already honoured, and the discovery content is a measurement capability and not a surprise from nature. Priority is also shared: Lemonde, Derevianko, Ludlow, Bloom, Takamoto and others made decisive contributions that a two-name credit leaves out, and the ion-clock lineage (e.g. Al+ clocks) is related. I also note that I am an atomic theorist, so I may find this case more natural than colleagues from other fields would.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy first (with Pearce) and values it as an invention that broke the Scherzer limit and opened atom-by-atom imaging; she declared her closeness to the field and holds it to a strict standard.
responses.response: I accept the scientific weight of this work and respect the honest declaration of proximity. The breakthrough is real and the maturity is beyond doubt. My reservation is about how it sits as a physics prize: it is an enabling instrument whose discoveries are made in materials science, and only two members support it, so it has not yet shown breadth across the committee. I also note Olsson and Pearce both flag that Krivanek's quadrupole-octupole corrector work is outside the credited trio, which makes the credit less clean than the clock pair. I would keep it as a serious contender for a later year, but I do not see it displacing the clock.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a new class of matter defined by band topology, with Kane and Mele for theory and Molenkamp for the HgTe observation, and values that electronic-structure theory predicts it quantitatively.
responses.response: I agree this is among the strongest conceptual results on the list and it is why I keep it as an alternative; I ranked it only sixth because condensed matter is outside my expertise and I defer to him on maturity, which he describes as secure. Where I qualify his case is credit: he himself notes that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe state and Fu, Hasan and others did the three-dimensional work, and the 2016 prize already honoured topology in matter. I would want the committee to be satisfied that a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio does not misstate the record before it ranks above a pair with no comparable dispute.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, as a new regime of strong coupling of an artificial atom to a microwave photon that underlies superconducting quantum processors, while acknowledging his proximity to the field and the overlap with the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I find the physics persuasive, since it is cavity QED in an unfamiliar guise and I know the atomic version well. But I share the concern he raises himself: the 2025 prize has just honoured macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits, and the theory credit among Blais, Girvin and Devoret is intertwined. Two other members (Kroll and Olsson) rank it low for the same timing reason. I would not argue it is less meritorious, only that the attribution and sequencing are less clean than for the clocks.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the TEM aberration correction trio and IceCube highly as detector-driven breakthroughs, and places the lattice clock third as a clean precision-measurement instrument with a clear pair of laureates.
responses.response: I am glad he sees the clock pair as clean and that he finds maturity unquestioned. On IceCube, which he ranks fourth and Danielsson ranks first, I agree it opened a real window, but he himself calls source identification thin and the recognition perhaps slightly early, and the collaboration scale makes personal credit hard. I would prefer to wait for that to settle rather than reward it ahead of a mature, repeatedly reproduced result.

responses.point: Kroll puts the lattice clock first as the clearest case of a technique that changed what can be measured, and ranks atom interferometry second, noting that Chu's earlier prize and omission complicate the interferometry story.
responses.response: We agree on the first choice and I think his view that a two-person prize is clean is correct. On atom interferometry I agree with his own caution: Steven Chu's 1997 prize and his light-pulse gravimeter work make the Bordé-Pritchard-Kasevich trio awkward, and I ranked it third mainly on scientific grounds. I therefore treat it as an alternative and not as a partner for the clock in a two-part prize, because the union would also exceed three people.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first and the Event Horizon Telescope second as direct windows on the universe, and notes that clocks overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that other clock groups may deserve credit.
responses.response: His overlap point is the right test and I take it seriously; my answer is that the comb prize rewarded the frequency ruler and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions, while the lattice clock is a different mechanism (a magic-wavelength trap with many atoms) that reached a different precision regime. I would, however, welcome a precise citation so the prize is not read as another general metrology prize. On the astrophysical candidates I defer to him and others on particle physics and astrophysics, but I would still be cautious about awarding individuals for collaboration-scale discoveries.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, or as their continuation.
Whether a third contributor (for example Pierre Lemonde or Andrei Derevianko) is needed, which the supplied credit does not address and I cannot verify here.
Priority between lattice clocks and single-ion optical clocks, which I cannot resolve from the files.
How the committee should weigh topological insulators, whose credit dispute I cannot judge from outside condensed matter.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier, a 2023 laureate, and have worked with Lund and ETH attosecond groups; this does not involve Katori or Ye, and my profile shows no specific personal or institutional connection to any shortlisted candidate. I work in atomic theory and in the same broad field as the clock candidate, which may bias me, and I flag that openly. No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile that would require recusal.
